title: Evolution
description: Grade 12 Biology: origin of life and evidences for evolution, Darwin's theory of natural selection, mechanisms of evolution, and a brief outline of human evolution.

topics.title: Origin of Life and Evidences for Evolution
topics.concept:
Evolution is the slow, gradual change in living organisms over very long periods of time, by which new species arise from earlier ones. It explains the enormous variety of life on Earth and how all organisms are related.

How did life begin? The widely accepted scientific idea is chemical evolution: the first simple life arose from non-living chemicals in the conditions of the early Earth. The Oparin–Haldane hypothesis proposed that simple molecules combined to form more complex organic molecules in the early oceans. The Miller–Urey experiment supported this by showing that, when a mixture of gases thought to be present on early Earth was given energy (sparks, mimicking lightning), simple organic molecules like amino acids were formed.

Several lines of evidence support evolution:

  • Fossils — the preserved remains of ancient organisms in rocks; they show how life forms have changed over time and reveal extinct species.
  • Homologous organs — organs with the same basic structure but different functions (e.g. the forelimbs of a human, whale and bat), showing common ancestry (divergent evolution).
  • Analogous organs — organs with different structure but the same function (e.g. the wings of a bird and an insect), showing similar adaptation to similar needs (convergent evolution).
  • Embryological and molecular evidence — similarities in early embryos and in DNA/proteins across species.

examples.problem: Example 1: What did the Miller–Urey experiment show?
examples.solution:
It tested chemical evolution.

  • Passing energy through early-Earth gases formed simple organic molecules (like amino acids).
  • This supported the idea that life's building blocks could form from non-living chemicals.
examples.answer: It showed that simple organic molecules (e.g. amino acids) could form from early-Earth gases given energy — supporting chemical evolution.

examples.problem: Example 2: What are homologous organs? Give an example.
examples.solution:
Same structure, different function.

  • Organs with the same basic structure but different functions.
  • Example: forelimbs of human, whale and bat.
examples.answer: Homologous organs have the same basic structure but different functions, e.g. the forelimbs of human, whale and bat — showing common ancestry.

examples.problem: Example 3: How do fossils provide evidence for evolution?
examples.solution:
Fossils are remains of ancient life.

  • They show how organisms have changed over time and reveal extinct forms.
examples.answer: Fossils are preserved remains of ancient organisms that show how life forms have changed over time.

recap:
• Evolution = gradual change in organisms over time; new species from earlier ones.
  • Origin of life: chemical evolution (Oparin–Haldane); Miller–Urey formed organic molecules from early-Earth gases.
  • Evidence: fossils; homologous organs (same structure, diff. function → common ancestry); analogous organs (diff. structure, same function → convergence); embryology & molecules.

quiz.q: The forelimbs of a human, whale and bat are examples of:
quiz.explanation: Same structure, different functions = homologous organs (common ancestry).

quiz.q: The Miller–Urey experiment supported the idea of:
quiz.explanation: It showed organic molecules can form from simple gases — chemical evolution.

topics.title: Theories and Mechanisms of Evolution
topics.concept:
The most important explanation of how evolution happens is Charles Darwin's theory of Natural Selection, put forward in his book On the Origin of Species (1859). Its main ideas are:

  • Organisms produce far more offspring than can survive, so there is a struggle for existence (competition for food, space, etc.).
  • Individuals of a species show variations; some variations are useful in the struggle.
  • Individuals with useful (favourable) variations are more likely to survive and reproduce — this is survival of the fittest, or natural selection.
  • Over many generations, the favourable variations accumulate, gradually changing the species and producing new ones.

An earlier idea by Lamarck (inheritance of acquired characters — e.g. the giraffe's neck lengthening from stretching) is now rejected, because changes acquired during life are not passed to offspring.

Today we understand the raw materials and forces of evolution more fully. Variations arise mainly from mutations (changes in DNA) and from the reshuffling of genes during sexual reproduction (recombination). Natural selection then acts on this variation. Other factors include genetic drift (random change in small populations) and migration. A simple example seen in real time is the way bacteria become resistant to antibiotics, or insects to pesticides: a few resistant individuals survive and multiply — natural selection in action.

examples.problem: Example 1: Who proposed the theory of natural selection, and in which book?
examples.solution:
Recall the founder of the theory.

  • Charles Darwin, in 'On the Origin of Species' (1859).
examples.answer: Charles Darwin, in his book 'On the Origin of Species' (1859).

examples.problem: Example 2: What is meant by 'survival of the fittest'?
examples.solution:
It is the core of natural selection.

  • Individuals with useful variations are more likely to survive and reproduce.
  • The less-fit are less likely to survive.
examples.answer: Individuals best suited (with favourable variations) survive and reproduce more, passing on their traits.

examples.problem: Example 3: Give a real example of natural selection seen today.
examples.solution:
Look for rapid selection.

  • Bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics (or insects to pesticides).
  • Resistant individuals survive and multiply.
examples.answer: The rise of antibiotic-resistant bacteria (or pesticide-resistant insects), where resistant individuals survive and multiply.

recap:
• Darwin's Natural Selection (Origin of Species, 1859): over-production → struggle for existence; variations; survival of the fittest; favourable traits accumulate.
  • Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characters = rejected.
  • Variation from mutation + recombination; also genetic drift, migration.
  • Real example: antibiotic/pesticide resistance.

quiz.q: The theory of natural selection was given by:
The main raw material for evolution (new variation) comes from:
quiz.explanation: Mutations (and recombination) create the variation selection acts on.

topics.title: Human Evolution
topics.concept:
Humans, too, are a product of evolution. Modern humans and the modern apes (like the chimpanzee and gorilla) share a common ancestor that lived millions of years ago — humans did not evolve from today's monkeys, but humans and apes evolved along separate lines from that shared ancestor.

The broad story of human evolution, pieced together from fossils, includes several stages:

  • Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus — ape-like ancestors; Ramapithecus was more man-like.
  • Australopithecus — early human-like forms in Africa that walked upright (bipedal) but had small brains.
  • Homo habilis — the "handy man," who could make and use simple stone tools; brain larger than Australopithecus.
  • Homo erectus — walked fully upright, had a larger brain, and is thought to have used fire.
  • Homo sapiens — modern humans, with a large, well-developed brain, language and culture.

The key trends across human evolution were: walking upright on two legs (freeing the hands), an increase in brain size, the making of better tools, and the development of language and culture. These changes gave humans their unique abilities. Human evolution is a powerful illustration of the same natural processes — variation and selection over long time — that have shaped all life on Earth.

examples.problem: Example 1: Did humans evolve from modern monkeys? Explain.
examples.solution:
Clarify the common-ancestor idea.

  • No. Humans and apes share a common ancestor.
  • They evolved along separate lines from that ancestor.
examples.answer: No — humans and modern apes share a common ancestor and evolved along separate lines from it.

examples.problem: Example 2: Which early human is called the 'handy man', and why?
examples.solution:
It used tools.

  • Homo habilis is called the handy man.
  • Because it could make and use simple stone tools.
examples.answer: Homo habilis, because it could make and use simple stone tools.

examples.problem: Example 3: List two major trends in human evolution.
examples.solution:
Several key changes occurred.

  • Walking upright on two legs (bipedalism), freeing the hands.
  • Increase in brain size (and development of tools, language).
examples.answer: Walking upright (bipedalism) and an increase in brain size (also better tools and language).

recap:
• Humans and apes share a common ancestor (not descended from modern monkeys).
  • Fossil stages: Dryopithecus/Ramapithecus → Australopithecus (upright, small brain) → Homo habilis (tool-maker) → Homo erectus (fire) → Homo sapiens (modern).
  • Trends: bipedalism, larger brain, better tools, language & culture.

quiz.explanation: Humans and apes evolved from a shared common ancestor.

topics.title: Modern Synthetic Theory, Hardy-Weinberg Principle and Adaptive Radiation
topics.concept:
Darwin explained natural selection but did not know about genes. The modern synthetic theory of evolution combines Darwin's natural selection with modern genetics. It views evolution as a change in the frequency of alleles (gene forms) in a population over generations, brought about by five main factors: mutation and recombination (which create variation), natural selection, genetic drift (random change in small populations) and gene flow (migration) — the movement of alleles between populations as individuals move in or out.

To describe a population that is not evolving, scientists use the Hardy-Weinberg principle. It states that in a large, randomly mating population with no mutation, no selection, no genetic drift and no gene flow, the allele frequencies stay constant from generation to generation (a state called genetic equilibrium). It is written as p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p and q are the frequencies of the two alleles. If the real frequencies change, it means one of the five evolutionary forces is acting — in other words, evolution is happening. So Hardy-Weinberg is a useful baseline for detecting evolution.

Adaptive radiation is the process by which a single ancestral species diversifies into many different forms, each adapted to a particular way of life (niche). The classic example is Darwin's finches on the Galapagos Islands, which evolved different beak shapes for different foods from one ancestor. The marsupials of Australia are another example. Adaptive radiation shows how evolution fills the variety of available habitats.

examples.problem: Example 1: What does the modern synthetic theory add to Darwin's idea?
examples.solution:
It brings in genetics.

  • It explains evolution as a change in allele frequencies.
  • Caused by mutation, recombination, natural selection, genetic drift and gene flow.
examples.answer: It combines natural selection with genetics, explaining evolution as a change in allele frequencies driven by mutation, recombination, selection, drift and gene flow.

examples.problem: Example 2: What does the Hardy-Weinberg principle state?
examples.solution:
It describes a non-evolving population.

  • In a large, random-mating population with no evolutionary forces, allele frequencies stay constant.
examples.answer: In a large, randomly mating population with no mutation, selection, drift or gene flow, allele frequencies remain constant (genetic equilibrium).

examples.problem: Example 3: What is adaptive radiation? Give an example.
examples.solution:
One ancestor, many forms.

  • It is the diversification of one ancestor into many forms adapted to different niches.
  • Example: Darwin's finches.
examples.answer: Adaptive radiation is the diversification of one ancestral species into many forms suited to different niches, e.g. Darwin's finches.

recap:
• Modern synthetic theory: evolution = change in allele frequencies via mutation, recombination, natural selection, genetic drift and gene flow (migration).
  • Hardy-Weinberg principle: allele frequencies stay constant (p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1) unless an evolutionary force acts — a baseline for detecting evolution.
  • Adaptive radiation: one ancestor → many niche-adapted forms (Darwin's finches, Australian marsupials).

quiz.q: According to the Hardy-Weinberg principle, allele frequencies in a population stay constant when there is no:
options: Mutation, selection, drift or gene flow
quiz.explanation: Equilibrium holds only when none of the evolutionary forces act.

quiz.q: The diversification of Darwin's finches into many beak forms from one ancestor is an example of:
quiz.explanation: One ancestor diversifying into many niche-adapted forms is adaptive radiation.

questions.explanation: Evolution occurs slowly over very long periods.

questions.explanation: It formed simple organic molecules from early-Earth gases.

questions.q: Preserved remains of ancient organisms in rocks are:

questions.q: Organs with the same structure but different functions are:
questions.explanation: Homologous organs share structure but differ in function.

questions.q: The wings of a bird and an insect (different structure, same function) are:
questions.explanation: Same function, different structure = analogous organs.

questions.q: The theory of natural selection was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Darwin proposed natural selection.

questions.q: Darwin's book on evolution is:
questions.explanation: Darwin wrote 'On the Origin of Species' (1859).

questions.q: 'Survival of the fittest' means individuals that survive and reproduce are those with:
questions.explanation: Those with favourable variations survive and reproduce.

questions.q: Lamarck's theory of inheritance of acquired characters is now:
questions.explanation: Acquired characters are not inherited, so the theory is rejected.

questions.q: The main source of new variation for evolution is:
questions.explanation: Mutations (and recombination) create variation.

questions.q: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria arise because resistant individuals:
questions.explanation: Resistant bacteria survive selection and multiply.

questions.q: Humans and modern apes:
questions.explanation: They evolved from a shared common ancestor.

questions.q: The early human called the 'handy man' (a tool maker) is:
questions.explanation: Homo habilis made and used simple stone tools.

questions.q: Modern humans belong to the species:
questions.explanation: Modern humans are Homo sapiens.

questions.q: Evolution, in the modern synthetic theory, is best defined as a change in:
questions.explanation: Evolution is described as a change in allele frequencies over generations.

questions.q: Movement of alleles between populations as individuals migrate is:
questions.explanation: Gene flow is the transfer of alleles between populations by migration.

questions.q: Homologous organs point to common ancestry, while analogous organs point to:
options: Convergent evolution toward a similar function
questions.explanation: Different structures evolving the same function (e.g. wings) reflect convergence, not shared ancestry.

questions.q: Overuse of antibiotics speeds up the spread of resistant bacteria because antibiotics act as a:
options: Cause of extinction of all bacteria
questions.explanation: Killing susceptible bacteria leaves resistant ones to multiply — natural selection in action.

questions.q: Lamarck's giraffe explanation fails because the longer neck gained by stretching during life is:
questions.explanation: Acquired characters do not change the genes, so they are not inherited — unlike heritable variation.

questions.q: The near-identical structure of forelimb bones in humans, whales and bats is best explained by:
questions.explanation: A shared underlying plan adapted to different uses indicates common ancestry (divergent evolution).

questions.q: Bipedalism (walking upright) was important in human evolution mainly because it:
options: Freed the hands for making and using tools
questions.explanation: Standing upright freed the hands, allowing tool use that drove further development.

questions.q: Random change in the gene frequencies of a small population, independent of fitness, is called:
questions.explanation: Genetic drift is chance fluctuation in allele frequencies, strongest in small populations.

questions.q: If the allele frequencies in a population are found to be changing over generations, it indicates that:
options: Evolution is occurring (an evolutionary force is acting)
questions.explanation: A departure from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium signals that an evolutionary force is at work.
